draft.title: How Mumbai University uses your personal data: your consent
draft.summary: Mumbai University is a university providing higher education. This notice explains, purpose by purpose, which personal data we would like to use and what each use does for you. We ask for your consent to each purpose separately. You may agree to some and not others. Where you are under eighteen, we ask a parent or lawful guardian to give consent for you.

purposes.title: Admissions
purposes.uses: Lets us check whether you are eligible for a course, verify your documents and keep you informed about your application. If the applicant is under eighteen, we ask for a parent's or lawful guardian's verifiable consent before using the applicant's data.
dataItems: Category certificate, where you apply under a category
Parent's or guardian's name and contact details

purposes.title: Examinations and results
purposes.uses: Lets us register you for examinations, conduct them, prepare and publish your results, and handle any request you make for revaluation.

purposes.title: Student records and administration
purposes.uses: Lets us manage your time as a student, from enrolment to completion, including your profile, attendance, fees and documents. If the student is under eighteen, we ask for a parent's or lawful guardian's verifiable consent before using the student's data.

purposes.title: Online learning
purposes.uses: Gives you access to the University's online learning platform, lets you submit assignments and join discussions, and lets teachers track your academic progress.

purposes.title: Scholarships and fee concessions
purposes.uses: Lets us check whether you qualify for a scholarship or fee concession and pay it into your bank account.
dataItems: Parent's or guardian's name and income details

purposes.title: Sharing records with affiliated colleges
purposes.uses: Lets the University and its affiliated colleges exchange your records so that your studies, examinations and required reports are managed correctly.
dataItems: Submissions made by your college about you

purposes.title: Automated help assistant
purposes.uses: Lets you ask questions of the University's automated (AI-based) help assistant and receive answers about courses, admissions and student services.
dataItems: Your contact details, only if you choose to give them

purposes.title: Event and webinar registration
purposes.uses: Lets you register for University events and webinars and receive joining details and updates about them.

purposes.title: Photographs at University events
purposes.uses: Lets us take photographs and video recordings at University events and use them to report on and promote those events.
dataItems: Video recordings in which you appear

purposes.title: Alumni updates
purposes.uses: Keeps you in touch with the University after you graduate, with news, updates and invitations to alumni events.

purposes.title: Alumni giving
purposes.uses: Lets us tell you about ways to support the University through donations.

law.point: A request for consent must come with or after a notice saying what personal data is used and for what purpose.
The notice must itemise the personal data and describe each specified purpose and what it provides or enables, in clear and plain language.
The notice must explain how to withdraw consent, exercise rights and complain to the Board; TrustStack prints this in fixed words, so the draft leaves it out.
Consent must be specific to each purpose and limited to the data needed, so purposes such as alumni updates and donations are asked separately.
Before using a child's data, the University must obtain a parent's or lawful guardian's verifiable consent.
Some uses, such as legal duties, State functions or employment, are legitimate uses that do not need consent and should not appear as consent purposes.
People must be able to read the notice in English or any language in the Eighth Schedule to the Constitution.
Rule 3 on notices applies from 13 May 2027.

missingInformation: The lawful basis for every record is undecided; counsel to confirm which purposes truly rely on consent and remove any that are legitimate uses under s.7 (for example examinations, statutory reporting or student administration).
Whether Mumbai University acts as a State instrumentality, which could make some processing a legitimate use under s.7(b) or s.7(c) rather than consent.
Faculty data in the online learning and affiliated college records may fall under employment use (s.7(i)); a person should confirm and keep it out of this student-facing notice.
Whether under-eighteens also use the chatbot, events or scholarships, which would need parental verifiable consent wording in those purposes too.
Whether the Fourth Schedule Part A exemption for educational institutions applies to any tracking or monitoring in online learning or student records.
Whether results are published publicly and in what form, which affects how the examinations purpose is described.
Which outside vendor runs the AI chatbot and what happens to chat logs, so the description is accurate.
Translations of the notice into the Eighth Schedule languages the University will offer.

draft.headline: All four penalty heads that apply are still at stake, mainly because the assessment is unfinished, so finishing it is the priority before 13 May 2027.
paragraphs: This brief is provisional. It rests on the assessment in progress, the Mumbai University DPDP Compass Baseline, where 123 questions are still unanswered. The processing register's gaps have never been generated. Many of the figures below will move as that work is done.

Statutory ceilings of ₹700 crore are at stake across 4 of 4 applicable penalty heads. This is the sum of the legal maximums in the Schedule to the Act (s.33(1)). It is not a predicted fine. The Data Protection Board of India (the regulator) decides any penalty only after an inquiry.

By head: security safeguards (₹250 crore ceiling) and children and lawful guardians (₹200 crore ceiling) are not yet assessed, because no question that evidences them has been answered. Breach notification (₹200 crore ceiling) is partially mitigated, assessed from 1 personal data breach in the breach register. Any other provision (₹50 crore ceiling) is exposed because 2 processors have no contract with DPDP clauses recorded. Significant Data Fiduciary duties do not apply, as no Government notification is recorded.

There are 203 days to 13 May 2027, when most of the DPDP Rules commence. Critical and high work has 3 items outstanding, and all work 4. The organisation is closing about 0 actions a week, against 0.2 a week needed to finish all work by that date. There is not enough history yet to forecast a finish date.
bullets: Ask the assessment owners to answer the 123 outstanding questions, starting with those that evidence security safeguards and children and lawful guardians.
Ask the register owner to generate the processing register's gaps for the first time, so exposure can be read from them.
Record contracts with DPDP clauses for the 2 processors that have none, or confirm with counsel what is in place.

law.point: The Data Protection Board of India may impose a monetary penalty up to the Schedule's ceilings only after an inquiry finds a significant breach and the organisation is heard.
The university, as Data Fiduciary (the body that decides why and how personal data is used), is responsible for compliance, including for processing by its vendors.
A Data Processor (a vendor processing data on the university's behalf) may be engaged only under a valid contract.
The university must take reasonable security safeguards to prevent a personal data breach; the Schedule sets the highest ceiling for this head.
After a personal data breach, the university must inform the Data Protection Board of India and each affected person.
The Board must be told without delay, with a detailed report within the period this rule sets unless the Board allows longer on written request.
Verifiable consent of a parent or lawful guardian is needed before processing a child's personal data.
After penalties in two or more instances, the Board may refer the matter so the Central Government can direct blocking of public access.
